issues.legal_issue: An ascetic member of a sect capable of owning property may hold personal property, and the claimant seeking possession must establish an entitlement to the property.
material_facts: The members of the relevant sect could own and acquire personal property, and some had been householders before becoming ascetics.
The predecessor ascetics received personal gifts and held inherited personal assets.
The plaintiffs claimed the disputed properties as belonging to the religious institution or its deity.
issues.conclusion: The ascetic status of a Mahant creates no presumption that property in his possession belongs to the Math or deity; there is no presumption either way, and the plaintiffs bore the burden of proving their entitlement.
issues.legal_principle: As stated in Sushil Chandra Sen v. Gobind Chandra Das and Gurcharan Prasad v. Krishnanand, members of certain ascetic sects may own personal property. The Court also relied on Dr. B.K. Mukherjee's Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trusts: a Mahant's ascetic status raises no presumption about whether property is personal or institutional, and the party seeking possession bears the burden of proving entitlement.

predicates.civil_property_ownership_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to ownership or possession of property.
predicates.ascetic_status_of_holder: The person holding the disputed property is an ascetic.
predicates.claimant_seeks_possession: The claimant asks the court to recognize an entitlement to, or order possession of, the disputed property.

issues.definition: When a property ownership claim seeks possession from an ascetic holder, the claimant must establish the claimed entitlement.

issues.legal_issue: Property acquired from a predecessor's personal assets remains personal property where the evidence, considered as a whole, does not establish that it was acquired from institutional funds.
material_facts: The disputed properties were purchased using a fund left by a predecessor Mahant, which included personal gifts and inherited personal assets.
The successor Mahant inherited that fund and used it to purchase the disputed properties.
The record did not establish that the Math's income left an appreciable surplus after its religious and other obligations were met.
Revenue records named the Mahant, rather than the Math or deity, as owner, and transfers of parts of the properties were not challenged.
The Mahant's will provided for the disputed properties to pass to the respondent.
issues.conclusion: The disputed properties were the Mahant's personal and separate properties, not properties of the Math or deity, and they devolved on the respondent under the will.
issues.legal_principle: Whether property was acquired by applying an institutional nucleus must be determined by considering all the facts and circumstances and balancing the entire evidence; no presumption applies either way, and the claimant bears the burden of proof. The Court relied on the principles stated in Sushil Chandra Sen v. Gobind Chandra Das and Gurcharan Prasad v. Krishnanand concerning personal property ownership by ascetics, and on Dr. B.K. Mukherjee's Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trusts concerning the absence of a presumption that a Mahant's property is institutional.

rule.if: civil_property_ownership_claim and purchase_funded_by_predecessor_assets and predecessor_assets_were_personal and not appreciable_institutional_surplus_shown

predicates.civil_property_ownership_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to ownership or possession of property.
predicates.purchase_funded_by_predecessor_assets: The disputed property was purchased using a fund left by a predecessor.
predicates.predecessor_assets_were_personal: The fund left by the predecessor consisted of personal gifts, inherited personal assets, or other personal wealth.
predicates.appreciable_institutional_surplus_shown: The evidence establishes that institutional income left an appreciable surplus available to fund the purchase.

issues.definition: In a property ownership claim, property purchased from a predecessor's personal assets is personal rather than institutional when no appreciable institutional surplus is shown.
